Appendix A CVaR Bounds Proofs

Theorem A.1.

Let XX and YY be random variables and ϵ∈[0,1]\epsilon\in[0,1].

  1. (1)

    Upper Bound: assume that P⁡(X≤bX)=1,P⁡(Y≤bY)=1P(X\leq b_{X})=1,P(Y\leq b_{Y})=1 and ∀z∈ℝ,FY​(z)−FX​(z)≤ϵ\forall z\in\mathbb{R},F_{Y}(z)-F_{X}(z)\leq\epsilon, then

    1. (a)

      If α>ϵ\alpha>\epsilon,

      (52) CVaRα⁡(X)≤ϵα​max⁡(bX,bY)+(1−ϵα)​CVaRα−ϵ⁡(Y).\CVaR_{\alpha}(X)\leq\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha}\max(b_{X},b_{Y})+(1-\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha})\CVaR_{\alpha-\epsilon}(Y).
    2. (b)

      If α≤ϵ\alpha\leq\epsilon, then CVaRα⁡(X)≤max⁡(bX,bY)\CVaR_{\alpha}(X)\leq\max(b_{X},b_{Y}).

  2. (2)

    Lower Bound: If P⁡(X≥aX)=1,P⁡(Y≥aY)=1P(X\geq a_{X})=1,P(Y\geq a_{Y})=1 and ∀z∈ℝ,FX​(z)−FY​(z)≤ϵ\forall z\in\mathbb{R},F_{X}(z)-F_{Y}(z)\leq\epsilon, then

    1. (a)

      If α+ϵ≤1\alpha+\epsilon\leq 1,

      (53) CVaRα⁡(X)≥(1+ϵα)​CVaRα+ϵ⁡(Y)−ϵα​CVaRϵ⁡(Y)\CVaR_{\alpha}(X)\geq(1+\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha})\CVaR_{\alpha+\epsilon}(Y)-\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha}\CVaR_{\epsilon}(Y)
    2. (b)

      If α+ϵ>1\alpha+\epsilon>1 and am​i​n=min⁡(aX,aY)a_{min}=\min(a_{X},a_{Y}),

      (54) CVaRα⁡(X)≥1α​(𝔼⁡[Y]−ϵ​CVaRϵ⁡(Y)+(α+ϵ−1)​am​i​n)\CVaR_{\alpha}(X)\geq\frac{1}{\alpha}\big(\mathbb{E}[Y]-\epsilon\CVaR_{\epsilon}(Y)+(\alpha+\epsilon-1)a_{min}\big)
Proof.

The strategy of the proof is to construct two distributions derived from FYF_{Y}, denoted FYLF_{Y}^{L} and FYUF_{Y}^{U}, such that FXF_{X} is stochastically bounded between them; that is, FYL≤FX≤FYUF_{Y}^{L}\leq F_{X}\leq F_{Y}^{U}. Consequently, since CVaR is a coherent risk measure, it follows that

(55) CVaRαFYL≤CVaRαFX≤CVaRαFYU,\CVaR_{\alpha}^{F_{Y}^{L}}\leq\CVaR_{\alpha}^{F_{X}}\leq\CVaR_{\alpha}^{F_{Y}^{U}},

where CVaRαFYL\CVaR_{\alpha}^{F_{Y}^{L}}, CVaRαFX\CVaR_{\alpha}^{F_{X}}, and CVaRαFYU\CVaR_{\alpha}^{F_{Y}^{U}} denote the CVaR at level α\alpha corresponding to the distributions FYLF_{Y}^{L}, FXF_{X}, and FYUF_{Y}^{U}, respectively.

Let amin=min⁡(aX,aY)a_{\min}=\min(a_{X},a_{Y}) and bmin=min⁡(bX,bY)b_{\min}=\min(b_{X},b_{Y}). Define the interval [bmin,bX)[b_{\min},b_{X}) to be ∅\emptyset if bmin=bXb_{\min}=b_{X}, and equal to [bY,bX)[b_{Y},b_{X}) otherwise. Analogously, define [amin,aX)[a_{\min},a_{X}) in the same manner. We then define upper and lower bounds for FYF_{Y} as follows (see Figure 15):

(56) FYU​(y)={0y<max⁡(aX,q1−ϵY)min⁡(FY​(y)−ϵ,1−ϵ)y∈[max⁡(aX,q1−ϵY),bm​i​n)1−ϵy∈[bm​i​n,bX)1y≥max⁡(bX,bY),F_{Y}^{U}(y)=\begin{cases}0&y<\max(a_{X},q_{1-\epsilon}^{Y})\\ \min(F_{Y}(y)-\epsilon,1-\epsilon)&y\in[\max(a_{X},q_{1-\epsilon}^{Y}),b_{min})\\ 1-\epsilon&y\in[b_{min},b_{X})\\ 1&y\geq\max(b_{X},b_{Y}),\end{cases}
(57) FYL​(y)={0y<am​i​nϵy∈[am​i​n,aY)min⁡(FY​(y)+ϵ,1)y∈[aY,min⁡(qϵY,bX))1y≥min⁡(qϵY,bX).F_{Y}^{L}(y)=\begin{cases}0&y<a_{min}\\ \epsilon&y\in[a_{min},a_{Y})\\ \min(F_{Y}(y)+\epsilon,1)&y\in[a_{Y},\min(q_{\epsilon}^{Y},b_{X}))\\ 1&y\geq\min(q_{\epsilon}^{Y},b_{X}).\end{cases}

As a first step, we verify that FYLF_{Y}^{L} and FYUF_{Y}^{U} are valid CDFs and that they satisfy FYL≤FX≤FYUF_{Y}^{L}\leq F_{X}\leq F_{Y}^{U}. To establish that FF is a CDF, it suffices to verify the following properties:

  1. (1)

    FF is non-decreasing;

  2. (2)

    F:ℝ→[0,1]F:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1] with limx→∞F⁡(x)=1\lim_{x\to\infty}F(x)=1 and limx→−∞F⁡(x)=0\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0;

  3. (3)

    FF is right-continuous.

Proof that FYLF_{Y}^{L} is a CDF:

  1. (1)

    On the interval [aY,min⁡(q1−ϵY,bX))[a_{Y},\min(q_{1-\epsilon}^{Y},b_{X})), the function FYLF_{Y}^{L} is monotone increasing, since FYF_{Y} is monotone increasing by virtue of being a CDF. Outside this interval, FYLF_{Y}^{L} is constant and consequently preserves monotonicity.

  2. (2)

    By definition, limy→∞FYL​(y)=1\lim_{y\rightarrow\infty}F_{Y}^{L}(y)=1 and limy→−∞FYL​(y)=0\lim_{y\rightarrow-\infty}F_{Y}^{L}(y)=0. We need to show that FYLF_{Y}^{L} is bounded between 0 and 1. By its definition, FYLF_{Y}^{L} is bounded between 0 and 1.

  3. (3)

    Within the interval [aY,min⁡(qϵY,bX))[a_{Y},\min(q_{\epsilon}^{Y},b_{X})), FYLF_{Y}^{L} is right-continuous since FYF_{Y} is right-continuous as a CDF. Outside this interval, FYLF_{Y}^{L} is constant and hence also right-continuous.

Proof that FYUF_{Y}^{U} is a CDF:

  1. (1)

    On the interval [max⁡(aX,q1−ϵY),bm​i​n)[\max(a_{X},q_{1-\epsilon}^{Y}),b_{min}), the function FYUF_{Y}^{U} is monotone increasing, since FYF_{Y} is monotonically increasing by virtue of being a CDF. Outside this interval, FYUF_{Y}^{U} is constant and consequently preserves monotonicity.

  2. (2)

    By definition, limy→∞FYU​(y)=1\lim_{y\rightarrow\infty}F_{Y}^{U}(y)=1 and limy→−∞FYU​(y)=0\lim_{y\rightarrow-\infty}F_{Y}^{U}(y)=0. By its definition, FYUF_{Y}^{U} is bounded between 0 and 1.

  3. (3)

    Within the interval [max⁡(aX,q1−ϵY),bm​i​n)[\max(a_{X},q_{1-\epsilon}^{Y}),b_{min}), FYUF_{Y}^{U} is right-continuous since FYF_{Y} is right-continuous as a CDF. Outside this interval, FYUF_{Y}^{U} is constant and hence also right-continuous.

Proof that FYL≤FX≤FYUF_{Y}^{L}\leq F_{X}\leq F_{Y}^{U}: To establish that FYL≤FX≤FYUF_{Y}^{L}\leq F_{X}\leq F_{Y}^{U}, we need to show that for all z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R}, FYL​(z)≥FX​(z)≥FYU​(z)F_{Y}^{L}(z)\geq F_{X}(z)\geq F_{Y}^{U}(z). Let z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R}.

  • •

    If z<am​i​nz<a_{min} then FYL​(z)=0=FX​(z)F_{Y}^{L}(z)=0=F_{X}(z).

  • •

    If z∈[am​i​n,aY)z\in[a_{min},a_{Y}) then FX​(y)=FX​(y)−FY​(y)+FY​(y)≤|FX​(y)−FY​(y)|+FY​(y)≤ϵ+FY​(y)=ϵ=FYL​(y)F_{X}(y)=F_{X}(y)-F_{Y}(y)+F_{Y}(y)\leq|F_{X}(y)-F_{Y}(y)|+F_{Y}(y)\leq\epsilon+F_{Y}(y)=\epsilon=F_{Y}^{L}(y).

  • •

    If z∈[aY,min⁡(qϵY,bX))z\in[a_{Y},\min(q_{\epsilon}^{Y},b_{X})) we assume that FY​(z)+ϵ≤1F_{Y}(z)+\epsilon\leq 1 because otherwise FYL​(z)=1F_{Y}^{L}(z)=1 and the inequality holds. FYL​(z)=FY​(z)+ϵ=FY​(z)−FX​(z)+FX​(z)+ϵ≥FX​(z)−|FY​(z)−FX​(z)|+ϵ≥FX​(z)F_{Y}^{L}(z)=F_{Y}(z)+\epsilon=F_{Y}(z)-F_{X}(z)+F_{X}(z)+\epsilon\geq F_{X}(z)-|F_{Y}(z)-F_{X}(z)|+\epsilon\geq F_{X}(z).

    If z≥min⁡(qϵY,bX)z\geq\min(q_{\epsilon}^{Y},b_{X}) then FYL​(z)=1≥FX​(z)F_{Y}^{L}(z)=1\geq F_{X}(z).

and therefore FYL≤FXF_{Y}^{L}\leq F_{X}. Note that the last proof holds when bX=∞b_{X}=\infty, making FYLF_{Y}^{L} a valid CDF when the support of XX is not bounded from above.

  • •

    If z<max⁡(aX,q1−ϵY)z<\max(a_{X},q_{1-\epsilon}^{Y}) then FYU​(z)=0≤FX​(z)F_{Y}^{U}(z)=0\leq F_{X}(z).

  • •

    If z∈[max⁡(aX,q1−ϵY),bm​i​n)z\in[\max(a_{X},q_{1-\epsilon}^{Y}),b_{min}) then FYU​(z)≤FY​(z)−ϵ=FY​(z)−FX​(z)+FX​(z)−ϵ≤|FY​(z)−FX​(z)|+FX​(z)−ϵ≤ϵ+FX​(z)−ϵ=FX​(z)F_{Y}^{U}(z)\leq F_{Y}(z)-\epsilon=F_{Y}(z)-F_{X}(z)+F_{X}(z)-\epsilon\leq|F_{Y}(z)-F_{X}(z)|+F_{X}(z)-\epsilon\leq\epsilon+F_{X}(z)-\epsilon=F_{X}(z).

  • •

    If z∈[bm​i​n,bX)z\in[b_{min},b_{X}) then FYU​(z)=1−ϵ=FY​(z)−ϵ=FY​(z)−ϵ+FX​(z)−FX​(z)≤FX​(z)−ϵ+|FY​(z)−FX​(z)|≤FX​(z)F_{Y}^{U}(z)=1-\epsilon=F_{Y}(z)-\epsilon=F_{Y}(z)-\epsilon+F_{X}(z)-F_{X}(z)\leq F_{X}(z)-\epsilon+|F_{Y}(z)-F_{X}(z)|\leq F_{X}(z)

and therefore FX≤FYUF_{X}\leq F_{Y}^{U}. Note that the last proof holds when aX=−∞a_{X}=-\infty, making FYUF_{Y}^{U} a valid CDF when the support of XX is not bounded from below.

Next, we derive bounds for the CVaR associated with FYUF_{Y}^{U} and FYLF_{Y}^{L}.

Upper bound for CVaRαFYU\CVaR_{\alpha}^{F_{Y}^{U}}: From Acerbi and Tasche, 2002, CVaR is equal to an integral of the VaR

(58) CVaRαFYU=1α​∫1−α1inf{y∈ℝ:FYU​(y)≥τ}​𝑑τ=1α​∫1−α+ϵ1+ϵinf{y∈ℝ:FYU​(y)≥τ−ϵ}​𝑑τ\displaystyle\CVaR_{\alpha}^{F_{Y}^{U}}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\int_{1-\alpha}^{1}\inf\{y\in\mathbb{R}:F_{Y}^{U}(y)\geq\tau\}d\tau=\frac{1}{\alpha}\int_{1-\alpha+\epsilon}^{1+\epsilon}\inf\{y\in\mathbb{R}:F_{Y}^{U}(y)\geq\tau-\epsilon\}d\tau

Theorem A.2.

Given the definition of X,Y,ϵX,Y,\epsilon and α\alpha as in Theorem 5.1, the lower and upper bounds of Theorem 5.1 converge to CVaRα⁡(X)\CVaR_{\alpha}(X) as ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0.

Proof.

Let ff and gg be continuous functions such that f⁡(0)f(0) and g⁡(0)g(0) are finite. Then limx→0f⁡(x)​g​(x)=(limx→0f⁡(x))​(limx→0g⁡(x))\lim_{x\to 0}f(x)g(x)=\big(\lim_{x\to 0}f(x)\big)\big(\lim_{x\to 0}g(x)\big). This property will be used throughout the proof.

Assume that FY​(z)−FX​(z)≤ϵF_{Y}(z)-F_{X}(z)\leq\epsilon for all z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R}. Since we consider the limit as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, we further assume that α>ϵ\alpha>\epsilon when computing the bound. Noting that CVaR is continuous with respect to the confidence level, it follows that limϵ→0CVaRα−ϵ⁡(Y)=CVaRα⁡(Y)\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\CVaR_{\alpha-\epsilon}(Y)=\CVaR_{\alpha}(Y).

(69) limϵ→0ϵα​max⁡(bX,bY)+(1−ϵα)​CVaRα−ϵ⁡(Y)=limϵ→0(1−ϵα)​CVaRα−ϵ⁡(Y)=limϵ→01−ϵα​limϵ→0CVaRα−ϵ⁡(Y)=CVaRα⁡(Y)\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha}\max(b_{X},b_{Y})+(1-\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha})\CVaR_{\alpha-\epsilon}(Y)=\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}(1-\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha})\CVaR_{\alpha-\epsilon}(Y)=\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}1-\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha}\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\CVaR_{\alpha-\epsilon}(Y)=\CVaR_{\alpha}(Y)

If FX​(z)−FY​(z)≤ϵF_{X}(z)-F_{Y}(z)\leq\epsilon for all z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R}, then, since we consider the limit as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, we assume in the derivation of the bound that α+ϵ≤1\alpha+\epsilon\leq 1.

(70) limϵ→0(1+ϵα)​CVaRα+ϵ⁡(Y)−ϵα​CVaRϵ⁡(Y)=limϵ→01+ϵα​limϵ→0CVaRα+ϵ⁡(Y)−limϵ→0ϵα​limϵ→0CVaRϵ⁡(Y)=CVaRα⁡(Y).\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}(1+\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha})\CVaR_{\alpha+\epsilon}(Y)-\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha}\CVaR_{\epsilon}(Y)=\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}1+\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha}\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\CVaR_{\alpha+\epsilon}(Y)-\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha}\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\CVaR_{\epsilon}(Y)=\CVaR_{\alpha}(Y).

Theorem A.3.

Let XX be a random variable, α∈(0,1],δ∈(0,0.5),ϵ=ln⁡(1/δ)/(2​n)\alpha\in(0,1],\delta\in(0,0.5),\epsilon=\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/(2n)}. Let X1,…,Xn​∼i​i​d​FXX_{1},\dots,X_{n}\overset{iid}{\sim}F_{X} be random variables that define the ECDF F^X\hat{F}_{X}.

Theorem A.4.

(Tighter CVaR Lower Bound) Let α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), XX and YY be random variables. Define a random variable YLY^{L} such that FYL​(y)≜min⁡(1,FY​(y)+g⁡(y))F_{Y^{L}}(y)\triangleq\min(1,F_{Y}(y)+g(y)) for g:ℝ→[0,∞)g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow[0,\infty). In order to prove that FYLF_{Y^{L}} is a CDF we need to prove that FYLF_{Y^{L}} is:

  1. (1)

    Monotonic increasing

  2. (2)

    F:ℝ→[0,1]F:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow[0,1], limx→∞FYL​(x)=1\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}F_{Y^{L}}(x)=1, limx→−∞FYL​(x)=0\lim_{x\rightarrow-\infty}F_{Y^{L}}(x)=0

  3. (3)

    Continuous from the right

Monotonic increasing: Note that for every fi:ℝ→ℝ,i=1,2f_{i}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},i=1,2 that are monotonic increasing, OPENf1​(f2​(x)))f_{1}(f_{2}(x))) is also monotonic increasing in x. Denote f⁡(x):=min⁡(x,1)f(x):=\min(x,1) and f2​(x):=FY​(x)+g⁡(x)f_{2}(x):=F_{Y}(x)+g(x). FY​(x)F_{Y}(x) is a CDF and therefore monotonic increasing, so f2​(x)f_{2}(x) is monotonic increasing as a sum of monotonic increasing functions. f1f_{1} is also monotonic increasing, and FYL​(x)=f1​(f2​(x))F_{Y^{L}}(x)=f_{1}(f_{2}(x)). Therefore FYL​(x)F_{Y^{L}}(x) is monotonic increasing.

Limits:

(75) 1\displaystyle 1 ≥limx→∞FYL​(x)=limx→∞min⁡(1,FY​(x)+g⁡(x))≥limx→∞min⁡(1,FY​(x))=limx→∞FY​(x)=1\displaystyle\geq\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}F_{Y^{L}}(x)=\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}\min(1,F_{Y}(x)+g(x))\geq\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}\min(1,F_{Y}(x))=\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}F_{Y}(x)=1

and therefore limx→∞FYL​(x)=1\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}F_{Y^{L}}(x)=1.

0\displaystyle 0 ≤limx→−∞FYL​(x)=limx→−∞min⁡(1,FY​(x)+g⁡(x))≤limx→−∞FY​(x)+g⁡(x)=limx→−∞FY​(x)+limx→−∞g⁡(x)=0\displaystyle\leq\lim_{x\rightarrow-\infty}F_{Y^{L}}(x)=\lim_{x\rightarrow-\infty}\min(1,F_{Y}(x)+g(x))\leq\lim_{x\rightarrow-\infty}F_{Y}(x)+g(x)=\lim_{x\rightarrow-\infty}F_{Y}(x)+\lim_{x\rightarrow-\infty}g(x)=0

and therefore limx→−∞FYL​(x)=0\lim_{x\rightarrow-\infty}F_{Y^{L}}(x)=0. By definition ∀x∈ℝ,FYL​(x)≤1\forall x\in\mathbb{R},F_{Y^{L}}(x)\leq 1, and ∀x∈ℝ,FYL​(x)≥0\forall x\in\mathbb{R},F_{Y^{L}}(x)\geq 0 because both g and FYLF_{Y^{L}} are non negative functions.

Continuity from the right: FYF_{Y} is continuous from the right because it is a CDF, and gg is continuous from the right by assumption. Their sum FY+gF_{Y}+g is therefore continuous from the right, and since the constant function 11 is continuous, FYL=min⁡(1,FY+g)F_{Y^{L}}=\min(1,F_{Y}+g) is continuous from the right as the minimum of two right-continuous functions.
Thus, FYLF_{Y^{L}} is a CDF.

FX​(x)≤FY​(x)+g⁡(x)=FYL​(x),F_{X}(x)\leq F_{Y}(x)+g(x)=F_{Y^{L}}(x),

and if FY​(x)+g⁡(x)≥1F_{Y}(x)+g(x)\geq 1, 1=FYL​(x)≥FX​(x)1=F_{Y^{L}}(x)\geq F_{X}(x). Therefore YL≤XY^{L}\leq X. ∎

Theorem A.5.

Let α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), XX and YY be random variables. Define h:ℝ→[0,∞)h:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow[0,\infty) to be a continuous function, g⁡(z):=∫−∞zh⁡(x)​𝑑xg(z):=\int_{-\infty}^{z}h(x)dx and YLY^{L} to be a random variable such that FYL​(y):=min⁡(1,FY​(y)+g⁡(y))F_{Y^{L}}(y):=\min(1,F_{Y}(y)+g(y)). We will show the g satisfies the properties of Theorem 5.3, and therefore this theorem holds. We need to prove that

  1. (1)

    limz→−∞g⁡(z)=0\lim_{z\rightarrow-\infty}g(z)=0

    g is continuous from the right.

  3. (3)

    g is monotonic increasing.

    FX​(y)≤FY​(y)+g⁡(y)F_{X}(y)\leq F_{Y}(y)+g(y)

It is given in the theorem’s assumptions that limz→−∞g⁡(z)=0\lim_{z\rightarrow-\infty}g(z)=0, so (1) holds. h is non negative and therefore gg is monotonic increasing, so (3) holds. gg is continuous if its derivative exists for all z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R}. Let z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R} and a<za<z.

(76) dd​z​g​(z)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dz}g(z) =dd​z​∫−∞zh⁡(x)​dx=dd​z​[∫−∞ah⁡(x)​dx+∫azh⁡(x)​dx]=dd​z​∫azh⁡(x)​dx=h⁡(z)\displaystyle=\frac{d}{dz}\int_{-\infty}^{z}h(x)dx=\frac{d}{dz}[\int_{-\infty}^{a}h(x)dx+\int_{a}^{z}h(x)dx]=\frac{d}{dz}\int_{a}^{z}h(x)dx=h(z)

where the third equality holds because ∫−∞ah⁡(x)​𝑑x=g⁡(a)\int_{-\infty}^{a}h(x)dx=g(a) is a constant that does not depend on z. The last equality holds from the fundamental theorem of calculus because hh is continuous. Finally, (4) holds because

≥P⁡(supz∈ℝ(F^Y​(z)−FX​(z))≤ϵ′)\displaystyle\geq P(\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}}\big(\hat{F}_{Y}(z)-F_{X}(z)\big)\leq\epsilon^{\prime})

From DKW Dvoretzky et al., 1956 inequality the following inequalities can be derived Thomas and Learned-Miller, 2019

(86) Pr⁡(supx∈ℝ(F^​(x)−F⁡(x))≤ln⁡(1/δ)2​n)≥1−δ,Pr⁡(supx∈ℝ(F^​(x)−F⁡(x))≥ln⁡(1/δ)2​n)≥1−δ.\Pr\left(\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\big(\hat{F}(x)-F(x)\big)\leq\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2n}}\right)\geq 1-\delta,\qquad\Pr\left(\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\big(\hat{F}(x)-F(x)\big)\geq\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2n}}\right)\geq 1-\delta.
(87) P⁡(supz∈ℝ(F^Y​(z)−FX​(z))≤ϵ′)\displaystyle P(\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}}\big(\hat{F}_{Y}(z)-F_{X}(z)\big)\leq\epsilon^{\prime}) ≥P⁡(supz∈ℝ(F^Y​(z)−FY​(z))+supz∈ℝ(FY​(z)−FX​(z))≤ϵ′)\displaystyle\geq P(\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}}\big(\hat{F}_{Y}(z)-F_{Y}(z)\big)+\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}}\big(F_{Y}(z)-F_{X}(z)\big)\leq\epsilon^{\prime})
≥P⁡(supz∈ℝ(F^Y​(z)−FY​(z))+ϵ≤ϵ+η)\displaystyle\geq P(\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}}\big(\hat{F}_{Y}(z)-F_{Y}(z)\big)+\epsilon\leq\epsilon+\eta)
=P⁡(supz∈ℝ(F^Y​(z)−FY​(z))≤η)>1−δ.\displaystyle=P(\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}}\big(\hat{F}_{Y}(z)-F_{Y}(z)\big)\leq\eta)>1-\delta.

The first inequality follows from the triangle inequality; the second holds since ϵ\epsilon bounds the distributional discrepancy between XX and YY; and the third follows from (86).

As with the preceding equations, all bounds in Theorem 5.1 hold deterministically for a given distributional discrepancy, where the discrepancy between F^Y\hat{F}_{Y} and FXF_{X} is ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime}. Consequently, the remaining probabilistic guarantees hold with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. ∎

Corollary C.4.

The bound from Theorem 6.2 holds for ϵ(bk,ak)=∑t=kT−1𝔼s[Δs(xt+1)|bk,ak]\epsilon(b_{k},a_{k})=\sum_{t=k}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}^{s}[\Delta^{s}(x_{t+1})|b_{k},a_{k}].

Proof.

As long as this discrepancy between their CDFs remains bounded by ϵ\epsilon, the result remains valid. Consequently, by bounding the belief-based discrepancy ϵ\epsilon in Theorem 6.2 via the state-based discrepancy bound established in Theorem C.2, we recover the same form of the bound for the newly defined ϵ\epsilon. ∎

From Theorem C.1, for all l∈ℝl\in\mathbb{R}

(137) |P(Rk:T≤l|bk,π)−Ps(Rk:T≤l|bk,π)|≤∑i=k+1T−1𝔼bk+1:i[Δs(bi,ai)|bk,π]=ϵ,\displaystyle|P(R_{k:T}\leq l|b_{k},\pi)-P_{s}(R_{k:T}\leq l|b_{k},\pi)|\leq\sum_{i=k+1}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}_{b_{{k+1}:i}}[\Delta^{s}(b_{i},a_{i})|b_{k},\pi]=\epsilon,

Appendix D Environment Configurations

The following subsections describe the three POMDP environments used throughout the experiments, including the action elimination experiments of Figure 9. Each domain provides an original environment (used for sampling rollouts) and a simplified surrogate (used for belief updates and CVaR bound computation). The two models differ only in their observation and reward models, as summarised in Table 1.

D.1. Light-Dark

State space: 𝐬=(x,y)∈ℝ2\mathbf{s}=(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} (2D continuous position). Action space: Discrete — {up,down,left,right}\{\text{up},\text{down},\text{left},\text{right}\}, mapped to unit vectors in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. Observation space: 𝐨∈ℝ2\mathbf{o}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} — noisy 2D position.

Original: Two independent 1D GMMs (one per axis), K=2500K=2500 components, approximating the target Normal distribution. Simplified: Standard Gaussian 𝒩⁡(0,σ2​I2)\mathcal{N}(0,\;\sigma^{2}I_{2}) with the same σ\sigma.

D.2. Continuous Push

State space: 𝐬=(rx,ry,ox,oy,tx,ty)∈ℝ6\mathbf{s}=(r_{x},r_{y},o_{x},o_{y},t_{x},t_{y})\in\mathbb{R}^{6} — robot, object, and target positions. Action space: Discrete — {up,down,left,right}\{\text{up},\text{down},\text{left},\text{right}\}, mapped to unit vectors. Observation space: 𝐨∈ℝ6\mathbf{o}\in\mathbb{R}^{6} — robot and target positions observed exactly; object position is noisy: o^=o+ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​I2)\hat{o}=o+\epsilon,\;\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{2}).

Original: One 1D GMM (K=7000K=7000 components) applied independently to each object-position axis; additionally adds stochastic reward noise 𝒩⁡(0, 25)\mathcal{N}(0,\;25). Simplified: Gaussian noise 𝒩⁡(0, 0.01⋅I2)\mathcal{N}(0,\;0.01\cdot I_{2}) on object position; deterministic reward.

D.3. Continuous Laser Tag

State space: 𝐬=(rx,ry,ox,oy,term)∈ℝ4×{0,1}\mathbf{s}=(r_{x},r_{y},o_{x},o_{y},\text{term})\in\mathbb{R}^{4}\times\{0,1\} — robot and opponent positions plus terminal flag. Action space: Discrete — {up,down,left,right,tag}\{\text{up},\text{down},\text{left},\text{right},\text{tag}\}. Observation space: 𝐨∈ℝ8\mathbf{o}\in\mathbb{R}^{8} — 8-directional laser range measurements with additive noise; terminal states return 𝐨=−𝟏\mathbf{o}=-\mathbf{1}.

Original: One 1D GMM with K=290K=290 components (σcomp=0.097\sigma_{\text{comp}}=0.097), applied independently to all 8 laser measurements; additionally adds stochastic reward noise 𝒩⁡(0, 0.25)\mathcal{N}(0,\;0.25). Simplified: Gaussian noise 𝒩⁡(0, 1.0)\mathcal{N}(0,\;1.0) per laser measurement; deterministic reward.

D.4. Shared Planner Parameters

These parameters are used in the open-loop bound evaluation experiments (Figures 9, 10, and 11) and in the closed-loop policy evaluation experiments (Figures 12, 13, and 14).

Appendix F BetaZero Policy Configuration (Light-Dark)

The closed-loop policy evaluation uses BetaZero Moss et al., 2024a, an AlphaZero-style algorithm for POMDPs. A neural network maps a belief summary vector ϕ⁡(b)\phi(b) to a scalar value estimate V⁡(b)V(b) and a policy prior π⁡(a∣b)\pi(a\mid b), which guide MCTS over particle beliefs.

F.1. Belief Representation

Particles are summarised into a fixed-size feature vector using the mean-and-standard-deviation representation:

(143) ϕ⁡(b)=[μ¯x,μ¯y,σ¯x,σ¯y]∈ℝ4,\phi(b)=\bigl[\bar{\mu}_{x},\ \bar{\mu}_{y},\ \bar{\sigma}_{x},\ \bar{\sigma}_{y}\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{4},

where μ¯\bar{\mu} and σ¯\bar{\sigma} are the weighted mean and standard deviation of the particle set.

Input normalisation is applied using online statistics collected during training:

F.2. Network Architecture

Two-headed MLP with a shared trunk and separate value and policy heads:

F.3. MCTS Parameters

F.4. Training Loop

At each episode, a fresh initial belief is sampled: mean ∼𝒰⁡([−1,8]2)\sim\mathcal{U}([-1,8]^{2}), std ∼𝒰⁡(0.01, 2.0)\sim\mathcal{U}(0.01,\;2.0), then Np=500N_{p}=500 particles are drawn from 𝒩⁡(mean,std2​I)\mathcal{N}(\text{mean},\;\text{std}^{2}I). This diversity prevents the training distribution from collapsing to a uniform loop.

F.5. Optimizer and Loss

F.6. Hyperparameter Search

The exploration constant cc and temperature τ\tau were selected via Optuna (TPE sampler, 20 trials) with nsim=100n_{\text{sim}}=100 during search:

Search used a MedianPruner (3 startup trials, 5 warmup steps) and a TPE sampler with seed 42. The objective minimised the final policy loss (cross-entropy vs. MCTS visit counts); the baseline uniform policy corresponds to ln⁡4≈1.386\ln 4\approx 1.386. The best trial was retrained at nsim=1000n_{\text{sim}}=1000 for the final model used in all experiments.

Appendix G Hardware Specifications

All simulations were conducted on a machine equipped with an 11th Gen Intel® CoreTM i9-11900K CPU running at 3.50 GHz and 64 GB of RAM.
